read_from: The route text as served: field 1 (the route text) of each row of reader/data/route-store of the main branch at commit 306f3b285898, store_version 87b13b1169b4 (its index.json), for "Brown-Driver-Briggs Hebrew Lexicon via Open Scriptures" (M5): 15,238 routes (axis: routes), 4,367 letters keys (axis: keys). The definition field of the same row is read only to understand a route, never classified. The source's own key to its signs: on file in part. The source's documentation, HebrewLexicon.pdf at commit 21c9add13bc727d3a951361778e97e3ff7afd1ce, and its schema BdbSchema.xsd stand at <tabernacle>/corpus-lane-builds/moses-works-own-stamp-v1/strand-1-the-old-books/fetch/ (M5-openscriptures-HebrewLexicon-21c9add.pdf.txt, M5-openscriptures-BdbSchema-21c9add.xsd). They settle what a route is: the def element holds a definition that BDB sets in bold or in italics, and "Normally, each in a series of definitions will have a separate" element. They say a list of abbreviations will come with the lexicon's prefatory material, and they name no sign of punctuation. The printed book's list of abbreviations stands beside them in an annex copy, hebrewenglishlex00browuoft_djvu.txt, a scan's text whose printing the source does not name: it gives fr. as from, obj. as object, and the mark on a shortened Hebrew word, and it was searched for the others. So the geresh shape cites that list, and every other shape whose words say what a sign is for begins "unverified:". The route text names neither the entry nor the element it came from; the lane read both from the dictionary store's records/M5.jsonl by audit (builder/source-audit.mjs), which is evidence about the source and no part of any test. By the audit (axis: routes): 15,238 of 15,238 routes are the whole text of one def element, 755 of them with the store's cut flag, and none is a part of one. So this dictionary is the case of the ask's second sentence, where the store already gives each tagged definition its own route: a list inside one route offers no second reading that a test can tell from a second wording, so no comma divides at rest and the lists wait in branches.

definitions.terms: In every test: a letter is any character of Unicode category L (JavaScript \p{L}), so the raised small e (U+1D49) and the Hebrew letters are letters; whitespace is what JavaScript's \s matches; a hyphen is U+002D only; an apostrophe is U+0027 only; the left single quote is U+2018 and the right single quote U+2019, and neither is an apostrophe; to trim is what JavaScript's String.trim does. Every match against a list is exact and case-sensitive, each entry as it is written with every character counted. To begin with an entry is a plain prefix: no word end is needed after it. The text is the route text untouched unless a test says to trim. What a bracket holds and the text before and after a mark are the template's c.group, c.before and c.after. At the start of the text there is no character before a mark and at its end no character after it, so a test that asks for a letter there fails and a test that asks for no letter there holds.
definitions.first_match: For each mark the shapes are tried in the order they stand in this file, and the first whose test holds names the occurrence; so each test speaks only of occurrences that no shape above it, for the same mark, has taken.
definitions.pieces: The pieces of a text: split the whole text at every comma and trim each part. A test that reads the pieces reads all of them, not only the two beside its own comma.
definitions.one_word: A piece is one word when it is not empty and holds no whitespace; a hyphen or an apostrophe inside it does not break it.
definitions.first_word: The first word of a text: the characters before its first whitespace, or the whole text if it holds none.
definitions.marked_rule: Each entry of marked_lists is one route's text, exact to the character and with nothing trimmed, with the three characters space, pipe, space written directly before each mark the entry marks. A text is marked when the whole text, untrimmed, is equal to an entry of marked_lists once that entry's ' | ' are taken out. An occurrence stands at a mark when its text is marked and in that entry a ' | ' stands directly before this occurrence: the occurrence's index in the text equals the index of that ' | ' in the entry less three for each ' | ' before it. A marked text's other marks do not stand at a mark. An entry may hold no ' | ': its text is marked and no mark of it stands at a mark.

homonyms.reason: The route text carries no entry number. The source's own file gives each of its 6,251 entries an id, and 1,084 of them a Roman numeral where BDB distinguishes entries that way (axis: records); the store dropped both, and the route text names neither, so two entries under one letters key stand there as separate texts with nothing to tell them apart (example key מלך: 10 route texts). keys_with_more_than_one_route_text counts senses and homonyms together. By the audit, of those keys (axis: keys) 1,647 are keys for which one single entry of the record yields every distinct route text, and 995 are keys for which no single entry does, so that the texts come from two or more entries that share the letters. Of those, 611 hold a root entry beside an entry of another kind, which can be a root and its own word and not two words (example key דקר: pierce under the root, piercing in the entry beside it), and 384 hold entries of one kind; the route text cannot say which of them are two words.

branches.question: Each row of this dictionary is one definition as the source's editors tagged it, and their notes say a series of definitions normally gets one tag each. Yet some tagged definitions hold a list with commas, some of them giving what a related word means in Arabic or Syriac. The commas asked about here each stand before a part that stands on its own, as in oppress, injure. The text cannot say whether a part is a second meaning or a second wording of one meaning, so the row stays whole until you answer. Does each comma of these lists divide? This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions, and a list with commas of both kinds cuts only at the commas this question rules.

options.means: Each comma this question rules cuts: the page prints oppress and injure as two readings. Each part prints as the source writes it, and a part that stands twice prints once.
No comma this question rules cuts: the page prints oppress, injure as one reading, as written.

branches.question: Some lists under one tag of the source, some of them giving what a related word means in Arabic or Syriac, share a word across their commas, like be firm, strong: the be serves both, so alone strong says strong where the source means be strong. In others a later word serves both sides, a part leans on words outside the list, or the last part is only half a word. Does each comma of these lists divide? This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions, and a list with commas of both kinds cuts only at the commas this question rules.

options.means: Each comma this question rules cuts: the page prints be firm and strong as two readings. Each part prints as the source writes it with nothing added, so a part can lack the word it leans on or be half a word.
No comma this question rules cuts: the page prints be firm, strong as one reading, as written.

branches.question: A few times two renderings under one tag of the source have no comma between them, only a semicolon, a question mark, a full stop or an & sign, like by means of what? how? Does that sign divide them? This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions: where commas stand beside the sign, they wait on their own questions.

options.means: The sign between them cuts: the page prints by means of what and how? as two readings. The sign at the cut is left out, and a sign at the very end stays.
The sign does not cut: the page prints by means of what? how? as one reading, as written.

branches.question: Two rows end in a comma or a full stop that the source's tag took in from the sentence around it and that is no part of the reading, like have a just cause, with its comma at the end. Should the page print that last sign? The stored text is kept either way, and this answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: The page prints the row as written, last sign and all: have a just cause, as one reading.
The page leaves off the last sign when it prints the row, a step of its own: have a just cause as one reading. The stored text does not change.

not_done_here: This ledger leaves to the route store which stretch of the source became a route: 14,322 routes (axis: routes) hold no mark at all, so nothing here rules them, and routes that are half a word, a single letter, a related word's meaning, a name's meaning or a verse's wording print as they stand whatever the commas do; a pointer at the end of a text would stay in the last piece, and no shape divides at rest.
